title: Code on Wages: minimum wage, floor wage and timely payment
author: Editorial Desk
summary: What the Code on Wages, 2019 changes for ordinary workers.
body:
The **Code on Wages, 2019** is one of the four Labour Codes that Parliament passed to replace India's scattered central labour laws. It deals with the most basic question in any job: what is the worker paid, when, and how is that pay protected? This post explains what the Code says in plain language, where it changes the older position, and what workers and unions are watching.

## Background: four laws, one Code

Before the Code, wage law was spread across four separate Acts: the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976. Each had its own definition of "wages", its own coverage, its own inspectors and its own penalties. An employer or a worker who wanted to know what was owed often had to read several Acts side by side. The Code of 2019 merges all four into one text with one definition of wages and one enforcement scheme.

The Code is part of a larger exercise. The Government consolidated 29 central labour laws into four Codes: on Wages, on Industrial Relations, on Social Security and on Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions. The Code on Wages is the oldest of the four, enacted in 2019, while the other three followed in 2020.

## A minimum wage for every employee

Under the old Minimum Wages Act, the right to a minimum wage applied only to workers in "scheduled employments", a list of occupations that governments had to notify one by one. One summary of the Code notes that this left roughly 30 per cent of the workforce covered. Many workers in small workshops, shops, agriculture and informal work were outside the list, or were inside it on paper but never reached by inspection.

The Code changes the starting point. The right to a minimum wage now extends to **all employees**, in the organised and unorganised sectors alike, without a schedule. Governments still fix the actual rates, and the rate can differ by skill, by area and by the nature of the work, but no employee is left outside the legal floor merely because the occupation was never listed.

## The national floor wage

The second big idea is the **floor wage**. The Central Government can fix a floor wage, which may differ for different geographical areas, taking into account the living standards of workers. The Code then says that no State Government may fix a minimum wage below that floor. If a State's existing minimum is lower than the floor, it has to be brought up.

The purpose is to stop a race to the bottom, where States compete for investment by keeping wages low. It is a floor, not a ceiling. A State is free to fix a higher minimum wage, and nothing in the Code lowers a wage that is already higher. For workers, the practical question will be how high the Centre sets the floor, and how often it is revised.

## One definition of wages

The Code gives a single definition of "wages". It covers all remuneration expressed in money, and then lists items that are left out, such as bonus, employer contributions to provident fund and pension, house rent allowance, conveyance allowance, overtime, commission, gratuity and retrenchment compensation.

The important safeguard is the **50 per cent rule**. If the excluded items together come to more than half of the worker's total remuneration, the excess is added back to wages. In plain words: if a worker's pay is Rs 100, at least Rs 50 must be treated as wages. An employer cannot show a small "basic pay" and pile the rest into allowances. This matters because provident fund, gratuity and several other benefits are calculated on wages, so a thin basic pay means thin benefits at retirement. Summaries of the Social Security Code note that the same 50 per cent test is used there for provident fund, ESI and gratuity.

## Timely payment

Delay in wages is one of the commonest complaints in factories, construction sites and security and housekeeping contracts. The Code sets due dates by wage period, as summarised in law-firm guides:

- daily wages are paid at the end of the shift;
- weekly wages are paid on the last working day of the week;
- monthly wages are paid by the seventh day of the following month;
- when a worker is dismissed, resigns, is retrenched or is otherwise removed, the final settlement is due within two working days.

Wages may be paid in cash, by cheque, by transfer to a bank account or digitally. Overtime must be paid at twice the normal rate, according to the summaries, and a worker who has not been paid on time can file a claim within three years of the date the wages became due, longer than the limits under the older laws.

## Bonus and equal pay

The Code carries forward the statutory bonus. Eligible employees receive an annual bonus of between 8.33 per cent and 20 per cent of wages, subject to the eligibility conditions and wage ceiling set in the Code. It also adds fresh grounds on which bonus can be denied, including sexual harassment, alongside fraud, violence and theft.

On equal pay, the Code bars discrimination on the ground of gender in wages for the same work or work of a similar nature, and it expressly covers transgender persons as well as men and women. The older Equal Remuneration Act spoke only of men and women.

## Who enforces it

The Code replaces the traditional "inspector" with the **Inspector-cum-Facilitator**. The facilitator is expected to advise employers and workers, guide compliance and help reduce disputes before penalties are used, and the system also allows web-based random inspections. Complaints about unpaid wages go to this officer. Beyond that, the appropriate Government, authorities hearing claims and, in the end, courts and tribunals are the forums for enforcement. Offences carry fines, and first-time offences that attract only a fine can be compounded at half the maximum fine. Repeat offences within five years cannot be compounded.

## Questions workers ask

- **Will my State's minimum wage fall?** The Code says the floor wage is a floor, not a ceiling. States cannot go below it, and they may go above it.
- **Does my allowance count as wages?** Only up to the 50 per cent rule. If allowances and other excluded items exceed half of your pay, the excess is counted as wages.
- **What if I am paid late?** Compare your pay date with the due dates above, keep proof of employment and payment, and approach the Inspector-cum-Facilitator or your union.

## What BMS says

In its pre-Budget letter to the Finance Minister on 6 January 2025, as reported by Organiser, BMS asked the Government to notify the Code on Wages and the Code on Social Security without delay, while seeking the removal of what it called anti-worker provisions from the other two Codes. It also said wages under MGNREGA should not fall below the minimum wage. BMS has long argued for a **need-based minimum wage**, meaning a wage worked out from what a worker's family actually needs to live decently, not from what an employer says it can afford.

## What remains to be done

A Code is only as strong as the rules, notifications and inspections behind it. Workers will be watching three things: the level at which the floor wage is fixed, whether State rules match the spirit of the Code, and whether the inspection system has enough trained officers to reach small employers. Unions have a role too, in making members aware of the due dates and the 50 per cent rule so that violations are reported.

## A later update

After this post was first written, the Ministry of Labour and Employment announced that the four Labour Codes would come into effect on 21 November 2025. Readers should check the notified Rules of the Centre and their own State for the current, detailed position.
